slides.headline: No, owls can't turn their heads 360°.
slides.sub: The real figure is about 270°, and their necks had to rewire to survive it

slides.headline: Its eyes are locked in place
slides.body: An owl's eyes sit in bony tubes and are virtually immobile. To look somewhere new, it turns its whole head instead.

slides.label: how far an owl can turn its head, in either direction
slides.body: Not a full circle. Johns Hopkins researchers studied the necks of snowy, barred and great horned owls that died of natural causes.

slides.headline: A twist that would hurt us
slides.body: In people, sudden neck twists can stretch and tear artery linings, causing clots and strokes. Owls twist much further without that damage.

slides.label: wider than the artery: the bony tunnels it runs through
slides.body: In 12 of an owl's 14 neck vertebrae, the holes carrying the vertebral artery are about 10 times its diameter, leaving room to move.
slides.source: de Kok-Mercado et al., Johns Hopkins (2013)

slides.headline: Built-in blood reservoirs
slides.body: Vessels under the jaw swell to pool blood for the brain and eyes mid-turn, and cross-links between arteries give blood a backup route.
slides.source: de Kok-Mercado et al., Johns Hopkins (2013)

slides.headline: Send this to someone who still says 360.
slides.body: Myths checked against the research. Follow @earthspirit_nature.
sources: de Kok-Mercado, Habib, Phelps, Gregg & Gailloud: Adaptations for owl head rotation, Science 339:514 (2013), via Johns Hopkins Medicine

caption:
Owls cannot turn their heads all the way round: barred owls (Strix varia) and their relatives manage about 270 degrees.

An owl's eyes are fixed in bony tubes, so the whole head has to move. A Johns Hopkins team used angiography and CT scans on a dozen snowy, barred and great horned owls to see how the neck survives it. One surprise: the vertebral artery enters the neck higher than in other birds, at the 12th vertebra rather than the 14th, which gives it extra slack.

Swipe for the four tricks that keep the blood flowing. Sources on the last slide.

Source: de Kok-Mercado et al. (2013), Science 339:514 and Johns Hopkins Medicine; Britannica.

Save it for the next time an owl does the head swivel.
